lessons.title: Sort, match and order
lessons.goal: Sort collections and compare small sets.
lessons.look: Aishatu's toy shop is open. The club needs to tidy leaf tickets and top counters for a new game. Mr Aliyu helps them sort and compare.
lessons.learn: A set is a collection. Sort by one rule: leaves together and tops together. Match one leaf to one top. Unmatched tops show which set has more. Sets with a partner for every object have the same number. Count sets and put them in order from fewest to most.
lessons.worked: Match 2 tops to 4 tops, one to one. Two tops in the set of 4 have no partner. Four is more than two; two is fewer than four. Sets of 2, 3 and 4 go in that order from fewest to most.
lessons.play: Sort clean, large leaves and large tops into separate sets. Match one leaf to one top. Say which set has more, fewer, or the same number. Swap roles. Make sets of 1 to 5 tops and order them from fewest to most.
lessons.hint: Read aloud and model sorting before matching. Put one object beside one partner; spacing and object size do not decide which set has more. Provide reachable materials and allow pointing, speaking or moving objects. Recheck later with fresh sets.

pages.title: Teach, notice and return
pages.subtitle: P1-02 / Sort, match and order / Mr Aliyu leads.

elements.text: Objective. Sort collections and compare small sets. Also retain the source ordering practice within 1 to 5. Read all pupil text aloud. Prerequisite: count objects to five; revisit the Chapter 1 model as needed. The pupil pages have no numbered instructions.

Concrete start. At a reachable table, provide three clean, large leaves and five large, clean tops. Use pieces too large to swallow; supervise use. These are pretend tickets and counters, not food. Sort by type in front of pupils, then invite them to sort a separate tray. A set means a collection. Reuse this same three-leaf/five-top tray for the ending. No pieces are added or removed.

Model, practise, compare. Enact p. 2 with real pieces before using the pictures. On p. 3 pair two tops with four, one to one, and point to the two unmatched tops. Name more and fewer. On the equal-row activity, invite a prediction, then match: all three have partners in both rows, so the sets have the same number even when spaced differently. On p. 4 count the dot sets 2, 3, 4 before connecting them to numerals. Read the numerals aloud.

Observe and help. Confuses type with colour: restate leaves together/tops together, sort one, then ask the child to place another. Counts twice: move each counted object aside. Chooses by row length: bring one object beside one partner. Gives a partner twice: physically move paired objects together. Cannot order: build sets of 1, 3 and 4, then compare adjacent sets. Recheck each difficulty with fresh small sets; accept speaking, pointing or moving objects before writing.

Recall and fresh checks. On p. 6 wait before offering help. After support, change the quantities (for example 1 and 2) and ask again. For this recheck, 2 has more and 1 has fewer. Keep p. 7 fresh tasks independent before feedback. On another day, ask what Mr Aliyu showed. Give four leaves and two tops to sort and compare, then ask pupils to order 5, 2, 3. Answers: leaves/tops; four leaves more, two tops fewer; 2, 3, 5. Record independent / with help / not yet.

pages.title: Answers and chapter notes
pages.subtitle: Adult task IDs preserve the six source questions; pupil tasks are unnumbered.

elements.text:
Every example and added task
p. 1 tray and p. 2 sort model: 3 leaves and 5 tops. Guided sort: the leaf in the second position is already circled; point to the leaf in the fourth position. Tops are first and third. Grace moves her leaf to the leaves.
p. 3 model: 2 matched pairs, 2 unpaired tops in the four-set; 4 more, 2 fewer. Guided rows: 3 in each, every top has a partner; same number. Any one-to-one bijection is valid.
p. 4 model: 2, 3, 4 dots in increasing order.
p. 6 support: 2 pairs and 1 unmatched lower dot; lower set of 3 has more. Accept either valid line from the remaining upper dot to a free lower dot.
p. 7 resolution: 3 pairs, 2 spare tops; tops more, leaves fewer. Put those 2 unmatched tops in a real spare box. Read the closing dialogue after doing this action.
p. 7 fresh sort: circle second and fourth objects (leaves). Fresh comparison: 5 leaves more than 4 tops; circle the right set.
P1-02-Q2 (p. 4): One dot in one set; three in the other.
P1-02-Q5 (p. 6): Exactly five objects.
P1-02-Q6 (p. 6): Match one to one or count both sets.

Words: sort = group by a rule; set = collection; match = pair one with one; more/fewer = greater/smaller number; same number = no unmatched objects. Historical source: original p. 1; objective/question links retained. Current curriculum comparison and Gombe educator review pending.

elements.text: Sequence. Pupil textbook pages 1-6: classroom purpose; two-to-none demonstration and the meaning of 0; guided one-to-none, recognition, numeral formation and empty-box drawing; independent source tasks; recall/support; actual packing resolution and fresh checks. Use the existing book introductions; this continuation does not repeat them.

Prepare. Large safe counters, reachable tray/mat, storage box, pencil/paper and ordinary cards 0-5. Demonstrate each physical action. The trays/boxes in exact diagrams are containers, not counted tops. Never count decorative classroom artwork. No subtraction or equality notation is needed in these pupil pages.

Notice. Separate empty-set meaning, recognition, independently naming a numeral, and writing without copying. A child may count the tray as one: ask what is being counted, then inspect its contents. An open or reversed loop needs formation practice, not a judgement that the child cannot understand none. Accept usual communication for naming; use an established adapted writing method where needed.

Intervene, then recheck. Use one counter and another container. Model moving it away and checking the contents. Link none to 0. Recheck independently with two counters and a fresh tray, both put away: zero remain. For writing, air-write and trace a large closed loop, cover the model, then dictate zero on blank paper. Give specific feedback and retry later.

Delayed recall. Next session put three counters in a different basket, then ask the pupil to put all away: zero remain. Mix cards 2,0,4: independently name two, zero, four without an adult supplying the names. Cover them and dictate zero: write 0. Record meaning, recognition, naming and formation separately; give further supported practice if needed.

elements.text: Sequence. TB1 purpose; TB2-3 quantities six/seven then eight/nine, numeral names and one-to-one counting; TB4 live formation/air-writing; TB5 actual sorting; TB6 modelled quantity order and source tasks; TB7 drawing model, recall/support; TB8 actual sorting/counting/ordering resolution, then fresh checks. Do not advance before each quantity is secure. Existing introductions remain in the opening book.

Prepare. Reachable mats, large safe counters, paper/pencil and cards 1-9. For S002 prepare 6 blue circles, 7 red squares, 8 green triangles and 9 yellow non-square rectangles. Model sorting by outline; shape naming is not assessed. Printed pieces use one colour to show the outline rule. All 30 pieces stay in the same four story groups. Squares remain a special kind of rectangle; use the most specific names here.

Separate skills. Observe quantity, count-once method, recognition, independent naming, dictation/formation and order separately. Counting correctly does not prove reading; copying does not prove writing from dictation. For reversed 6 or 9, keep paper upright and watch the loop/downstroke. Accept usual communication and established adapted writing methods.

Support/recheck. Use counted/uncounted mats and five counters plus one. Model six, then independently check a new seven set. If sorting is hard, sort two small groups then rebuild the target groups. For numeral difficulty, air-write/trace one form, cover it, then dictate it; later retry a different order. Do not label a child as the weak counter.

Delayed recall, next session. Count fresh sets of 6, 7 and 8. Read shuffled cards 9, 6, 8, 7 independently. Dictate nine, seven, six, eight: 9, 7, 6, 8. Order 8, 6, 9: 6, 8, 9. Sort 7 tops and 9 leaves; state each count. Record which skills need support.

elements.text: Source tasks. P1-04-Q1 (TB6/WB2): 7. Q2 (same): 8. Q3 (same): 6, 7, 8, 9. Q4 (TB7/WB3): exactly 6 separate dots, any clear arrangement. Q5 (same): exactly 9 real objects, each counted once; state 9. Q6 (TB7/WB4): recount 8 once per object; the last word is eight. Moving each counted object is valid. Check the method as well as the total.

Every model. TB2: 6 is five and one; 7 is five and two. TB3: 8 is five and three; 9 is five and four. Spreading changes no quantity. TB4/WB1: recognisable 6, 7, 8, 9; loop below for 6, above for 9. TB5: 6 round/7 square; guided 8 triangle/9 rectangle. TB6: pairing 6 and 7 leaves one unmatched in 7; seven goes between six and eight. Before/after mean earlier/later in counting order. TB7: 2 counters/2 dots; support 6, recheck 7. TB8: groups of 6, 7, 8, 9 in increasing row order.

S002 (TB5/WB5). Mix all 30 pieces. Sort by outline, count and record: 6 circles, 7 squares, 8 triangles, 9 non-square rectangles. Order: 6, 7, 8, 9. Observe actual sorting; written counts alone do not demonstrate it. For story closure (TB8), verify all 30 pieces in these groups before starting the pretend game.

Fresh checks (TB8/WB6). Privately prepare new scattered groups of 8 and 9; answers 8 and 9. S003: count 9 objects once each, then independently name ALL shuffled cards 1-9 without supplied names. Test recognition separately by naming 6, 7, 8, 9 in a different order. Before dictation, cover ALL cards, printed numerals and the pupil's handwritten count answers, including the totals on WB6. S004: dictate eight, six, nine, seven; answers 8, 6, 9, 7, correctly oriented. Do not show answers or read this rubric aloud while testing.
Same tasks on both surfaces count as one check. New physical objects, independently shuffled naming and covered-model dictation are fresh evidence. No tasks have been administered to pupils.

Tell or show your partner before getting a hint.

Choose a number from eleven to nineteen.
Write it in your exercise book. Build it with real strips.
Record its tens and ones. Explain how they match your number.

Adamu: I will check a bundle, then give my partner a turn.
Grace: We can open it and count the ones inside.

Need help? With an adult, count nine strips. Add one more and count them all. Tie these ten as one bundle.
Open it and check again. Then an adult gives you a new small set to bundle and record on your own paper.

For writing, practise the digits in their places. Cover the model and earlier answers before a new try.

elements.text: Progression. TB1 purpose; TB2 ten ones, bundle/unbundle without changing quantity; TB3 tens on left/ones on right; TB4-5 gradual building/naming of every number 11-20; TB6 live formation/reading; TB7-8 source tasks; TB9 recall/support; TB10 actual packing and fresh checks. Do not rush a ladder page as one lesson. Teach each number with real materials before proceeding.

Prepare. Large paper strips, loose bands, reachable trays/box, pencil/paper and ordinary cards 10-20. Keep 20 strips for the story; use extra demonstration strips or return all story strips before closure. Every tied ten contains exactly 10 visible/countable strips. The band is not one of the counted strips. Open bundles to verify rather than trusting labels or decorative art.

Observe separately. Does the pupil count each one once, make exactly ten, preserve quantity on tying/untying, read shuffled numerals, place digits correctly and explain zero loose ones in 20? One bundle is one ten, not one one. The left digit counts tens, the right counts loose ones. For 10 versus 1, compare actual ten strips with one strip. Accept usual communication and established adapted writing methods.

Help and fresh recheck. Count 9 then one more, recount 10, tie and open. Privately prepare a different set of 11 or 13 strips. Ask for complete tens and loose ones, then a record: 11 gives 1 ten/1 one; 13 gives 1 ten/3 ones. Give no answer before the attempt. For handwriting, model one two-digit numeral, cover all models and prior answers, then dictate a different one on fresh space.

Delayed recall. Next session build 18 (1 ten and 8 ones) and 10 (1 ten and 0 ones). Read shuffled 19, 12, 20, 11. Cover cards and every prior written/printed numeral, then dictate fifteen, twenty, eleven: 15, 20, 11. Record distinct skill results and revisit difficulties.

elements.text: Source questions. P1-05-Q1 (TB7/WB2): 12. Q2 (same): 1 ten and 6 ones. Q3 (same): 10 ones. Q4 (TB8/WB4): 19. Q5 (same): 2 bundles, exactly 10 ones in each; 20 total. Q6 (same): ten has 10 ones; one has 1 one. An opened real bundle or accurate pointing/explanation is acceptable.

All models/practice. TB2: 10 loose becomes one ten, still 10 after untying. TB3: 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones; guided 13 is 1 ten and 3 ones. TB4: 11-15 have 1 ten and 1-5 loose ones respectively. TB5: 16-19 have 1 ten and 6-9 ones respectively; 20 has 2 tens and 0 ones. TB6 cards name eighteen, eleven, twenty, sixteen. WB1: 10 ones; two tens and no loose ones make 20. WB3: form 10, 14, 20. Digits must be recognisable and in order.

Recall/choice/support/ending. TB9/WB5: open/count 10 once each. Any chosen 11-19 is valid: 1 ten and the remaining 1-9 ones; written numeral, real strips and recorded digits must agree. Support/recheck is described on TB11. TB10 ending uses the original 20 markers: exactly 10 in each of 2 bundles, no loose ones. Actually pack/check before closure.

Fresh checks (TB10/WB6). Privately ask pupil to build 17 and 20: 1 ten/7 ones and 2 tens/0 ones; open/recount to check. Shuffle ALL cards 10-20 for independent naming without supplied names. Test recognition separately by naming 10, 16, 20 in a different order. Before dictation cover ALL cards, printed numerals and earlier handwritten answers, including WB6 build records. Dictate nineteen, ten, fourteen, twenty: 19, 10, 14, 20. Do not show this rubric while testing.
Repeated tasks on two surfaces are one check. Models are not fresh assessment evidence. Variable pupil-built sets require observation. No classroom outcomes are asserted.

elements.text: Words. One: a single item here. Ones/units: single items. A ten contains ten ones; the ones place records loose ones. Bundle of ten: exactly ten ones held together. Tens place: the left position in our two-digit numbers; ones place: the right. Zero ones: no loose ones. Eleven to nineteen: one ten and one to nine extra ones. Twenty: two tens.

Historical mapping. P1-p02-06: recognise ten objects as one group. P1-p02-07: tens/ones with activities extending to 20. Stable P1-05-Q1-Q6 prompts, answers and order retained. Explicit quantity/naming/formation practice through 20 implements the adopted annual progression; this does not establish current curriculum alignment.

Provenance. Existing fictional Mrs Binta classroom asset reused: artwork/redesign/scenes/mrs-binta-blackboard-v1.png, with original image_gen prompts/references in adjacent provenance and artwork/manifest.json. No new AI art. Every assessed strip/bundle is a deterministic vector drawing; the bundle always shows ten separate strips. Fonts: DejaVu Sans; fonts/LICENSE_DEJAVU.txt.

Limits. Historical baseline plus documented provisional assumptions. Current applicable curriculum/Gombe adoption, local educator/pupil trials, accessible-PDF certification, physical print proof and printer approval remain pending. No device is needed; ordinary paper, safe strips and bands suffice.

elements.text: Prepare. Large safe strips, bands, reachable trays, three boxes, cards 1-99, paper and pencils. A bundle is ten separate strips. Open and recount it. The binding is not counted. Artwork is decorative; exact mathematics uses vector diagrams or actual strips.

Progression. Prior 1-20 check first. Re-teach any gaps before larger numbers. Use several sessions for 21-25, then 26-29, then each decade through 99. For EVERY number in a band, model build/name/formation, build/read/write together, then independent samples. Do not present the band list as one rapid lesson. All numerals use already-taught digits 0-9; demonstrate live formation and spacing again as needed.

Distributed WB checks. Use these band lists in order. Read cards: 25/21/24;29/26/28;39/30/38;49/40/48;59/50/58;69/60/68;79/70/78;89/80/88;99/90/98. Recognise the middle card among:21/22/25;26/27/29;30/31/39;40/41/49;50/51/59;60/61/69;70/71/79;80/81/89;90/91/99. Dictation lists and build/count answers follow on the next page. Cover ALL cards, models and earlier handwriting before dictation. Use fresh space or extra paper. Record count/build/read/recognition/copy/memory-writing separately. Read-aloud cards are visual stimuli, so remain visible only during reading/recognition.

Prior check. Count 7; build 12 and 20; read 5,19,2,10,16; recognise spoken 19 among 12,19,20; after copying 12 cover it and dictate fifteen (15). These are prerequisite samples, not complete 1-20 mastery. Later rotate all earlier values 1-20 across oral counting, mixed reading and covered writing.
Access. Speaking, pointing or moving strips can show understanding. An adult may scribe explanations. Record assisted handwriting separately; do not mistake a motor difficulty for a number error.

elements.text: Source answers. Q1 46. Q2 eighty-one (spoken acceptable). Q3 40, 41. Q4 9 tens and 3 ones. Q5 95,96,97,98,99 in order, including both endpoints. Q6 60 is six tens (sixty ones); 6 is six ones. Practical bundles or clear explanation are valid.

Models/guided. 14=one ten/four ones; twenty=two tens/no ones. For every two-digit model, count the bundles to check the tens digit and count the loose strips to check the ones digit. Read the printed whole name. Nine loose ones plus one makes ten loose ones; exchanging makes one more ten and zero loose ones. At transitions 29/39/49/59/69/79/89 become 30/40/50/60/70/80/90. Sequence model 29; guided gaps 50,51; 72 is 7 tens/2 ones; 84 is 8 tens/4 ones; range 62,63,64,65.

Every band WB. Build/count totals respectively: 22/23, 27/28, 31/32, 41/42, 51/52, 61/62, 71/72, 81/82, 91/92. Accept clear bundles of ten and remaining ones. Read cards in each stated order with the correct whole names. Recognition targets:22,27,31,41,51,61,71,81,91. Dictation answers: 24,25; 28,29; 33,39; 43,49; 53,59; 63,69; 73,79; 83,89; 93,99. Copied numbers must match each model; memory trials must be covered.

Names/recall/story. Teen/tens pairs have one ten plus the stated loose ones versus 3-9 tens/no ones; fourteen/forty, fifteen/fifty, sixteen/sixty, seventeen/seventy, eighteen/eighty, nineteen/ninety. For any chosen number21-99, bundles and loose ones must total that number and its whole name must be correct. Recall: count/check ten, tie, retain same total. elements.text: Fresh checks. Count a prepared 47-strip set (4 checked tens,7 loose). Build spoken thirty-six and eighty-two (3t6o;8t2o). Read shuffled 24,39,40,57,68,70,86,99 aloud: twenty-four, thirty-nine, forty, fifty-seven, sixty-eight, seventy, eighty-six, ninety-nine. Recognise spoken fifty-three among cards 35,53,50. Hide ALL cards, printed models and earlier handwriting; dictate twenty-three, thirty-eight, forty, fifty-six, sixty-seven, seventy-one, eighty-five, ninety-nine: 23,38,40,56,67,71,85,99. Use extra paper; split into brief sessions.

Misconceptions and intervention. A bundle mistaken for one: open and count ten. Reversed digits: build 24, touch two tens/four ones, record places. Teen/tens confusion: contrast 13 and 30 physically; stress whole name. After 29, child says 210: tie the ten loose ones; record 3 tens/0 ones. Zero ignored: compare 60 with 6 physically. Repeat with support, then privately recheck NEW 34 (3t4o), 50 (5t0o), read 17/70, dictate thirty-two (32) after covering. Do not award independent success for the coached example.

Delayed recall next session. Build 58 (5t8o); count prepared 64 (6t4o); read shuffled 31,49,50,62,79,80,95: thirty-one, forty-nine, fifty, sixty-two, seventy-nine, eighty, ninety-five. Recognise ninety-two among 29,92,90. Cover all models/earlier writing; dictate 29,30,44,59,60,78,90,96 using spoken names. Continue new samples in every band and 1-20 in later weeks. A small sample never establishes full-range mastery.

Record. Note independent/assisted/not yet for each mode, date and response. Copying alone does not establish memory writing; pointing alone does not establish naming. No pupil outcomes have been claimed.

elements.text:
Equal parts.
Fair shares.

Aishatu: My box-toy display needs one paper mat. Each of us wants the same space for a drawing. I want to start now!
Mrs Binta: First let us learn to share the whole mat fairly.
Adamu: Nobody should be left out.
Grace: I will check the edges neatly.
John: Let me try a fold before you tell me.
We will make and recognise equal halves and quarters. Keep paper on a reachable table. Use scrap paper instead of food.

textbook_pages.title: Watch the paper fold
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: This complete sheet is one whole. Watch me bring one short edge exactly onto the other. Press the fold. Open the sheet.
The line shows the fold. The two pieces cover the same amount of paper. Fold again to check that they fit exactly on each other. Equal means the same amount of space here.
Each part is a half of the whole. Two equal halves make the whole. I shade one part on my paper: one half is shaded.
Try together. Take a rectangle of scrap paper. Match its short edges, fold and open. Touch each half. Say, "Two equal parts." Turn the sheet. Is each part still a half?
Grace: Turning the sheet changes its direction. It does not change the amount of paper in each half. Keep your folded sheet for the next turn.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter seven / Equal halves and quarters
textbook_pages.title: Fold again for quarters
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch with a square sheet. Match opposite edges and fold in half. Keep it folded. Match the other pair of edges and fold once more. Open all the folds.
There are four equal parts. Each part is a quarter of the whole. Four equal quarters make the whole. I shade just one part: one quarter is shaded.
Try together. Fold your own square in half, then fold it in half again the other way. Open it. Touch and count the four equal parts. Shade one part on your paper.
Adamu: I count four parts. Mrs Binta: Check the amount too. Fold them onto each other: they must fit. Four pieces alone do not prove that they are quarters.

elements.text:
Aishatu: I drew a quick line. Two pieces must be halves!
Mrs Binta: Check them. One has less paper. Two unequal pieces are not halves.
John: The right whole has two equal parts. Each is a half. Aishatu tries again and matches the edges before pressing the fold.
A new way: I draw a line from one corner of a square to the opposite corner. The two triangles fit exactly on each other when folded. Each triangle is a half.
Try together. On paper, copy the square and corner-to-corner line. Point to a half. Explain how the pieces match. Workbook: Check the parts.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch me turn a square without changing its pieces. In the tilted square, four equal triangles meet in the middle. One shaded triangle is a quarter.
The paper orange model also has two equal parts. One part is a half. It is paper, not food. Fold a round paper model through its centre to check the matching halves.
Say together: a half is one of two equal parts; a quarter is one of four equal parts. Shape and direction may change. Equal amounts still matter.
Mrs Binta: Now we can read short names. 1/2 is read "one half": one of two equal parts. 1/4 is read "one quarter": one of four equal parts. Say the words as I point. You may answer in words.

Watch me draw a square. I draw one line through the middle from top to bottom, then another from side to side. I count four equal parts. I shade just one.

elements.text: Source questions (textbook p7; workbook pp2-3). Q1: 2 equal parts. Q2: 4 equal parts. Q3: rectangle divided into two equal-area parts; middle vertical/horizontal or corner-to-corner diagonal accepted. Q4: square with four equal-area parts, exactly one shaded; grid or four centre-meeting triangles accepted. Q5: No; unequal amounts are not halves. Q6: whole has four equal parts and exactly one is shaded. Accept equivalent spoken wording.

Models and guided turns (textbook pp2-6; workbook p1). HALF: two matching equal parts, unchanged when turned. QUARTER: four matching parts after perpendicular folds, one shaded. COMPARE: left .3/.7 unequal, right .5/.5 halves. DIAGONAL: two equal triangles each half. ROTATED: four equal triangles, one shaded quarter. FRUIT: two equal parts, one shaded half. NOTATION: 1/2 one half; 1/4 one quarter. DRAW: rectangle middle line; square middle cross with one part shaded. Workbook p1: top-left half, top-right quarter; bottom-left no, bottom-right yes. Require amount as well as count.

Support, recheck and extension (textbook p8; workbook p4). Helped rectangle: two equal halves. New tall rectangle: one middle line makes equal halves; new square: four equal parts, one indicated quarter. A different half may be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. Test equal area by folding/overlay, not matching shape alone; different-shaped pieces can also have equal area. Adults may verify other mathematically valid partitions.

textbook_pages.title: Story, fresh checks and delayed recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult reference / Read with both exact chapter books.

elements.text: Story (textbook p9; workbook p5). One square whole, four equal quarters, one drawing per friend. Four quarters exhaust the whole with no overlap. Names on textbook mat: Aishatu upper-left, Adamu upper-right, Grace lower-left, John lower-right. Workbook may place names or drawings in any order. Require one equal share for each, no excluded friend.

Fresh tasks (textbook p10; workbook p6). Left: half, two equal parts, one shaded despite rotation. Middle paper fruit: quarter, four equal parts, one shaded. Right: neither, two unequal parts (.3/.7); shading alone does not name a fraction. New drawing: four equal-area parts of a whole with exactly one shaded. Recall: half one of two equal parts; quarter one of four equal parts.

Intervene, then new recheck. If counting alone: overlap unequal paper pieces to show unequal space. Match folded edges before naming halves. If all shaded parts called quarters: compare equal two-part and equal four-part wholes, touching each part. If rotation confuses: turn the same sheet slowly. After help, give a NEW wide rectangle for halves and NEW square for quarters. Do not score coached work as independent.

Delayed recall next session. With blank paper and no models, ask the pupil to make equal halves of a new rectangle and quarters of a new square, point to one part of each and explain. Present a square split diagonally and a paper orange split into unequal pieces: half; not halves. Check again in later weeks with different orientations. Record assistance.

elements.text: Glossary. Whole: the complete object or shape being shared. Equal parts: parts with the same amount of area (space inside the shape). Half: one of two equal parts of a whole. Quarter: one of four equal parts. Fold: bend paper so parts lie on each other. Unequal: different amounts. Symbols 1/2 and 1/4 are read only after concrete models; symbol writing is not required here.

elements.text:

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Here are Aishatu's two tops and Adamu's one top. The pictures show the same tops before and after moving them.
Before: two tops
and one top

I touch each top once: one, two, three. The last count tells how many altogether. Two and one make three tops.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: We have joined the tops. Now we can write that story.

The plus sign + means add: put amounts together.
The equals sign = means has the same value as. Two plus one has the same value as three.

Grace: I thought equals meant "write an answer next".
Mr Aliyu: It tells us both sides have the same value. We can also write 3 = 2 + 1.
Try together. Put one counter beside two counters. Count all. Say "one plus two equals three". Check both sides have three counters altogether.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Keep our three stall tops aside. Use separate practice counters now. Join one, one and two counters. Count all four. We write 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.
Now watch a larger three-set example with practice counters. Two, two and two join. Touch each once: one, two, three, four, five, six.
2 + 2 + 2 = 6. Two plus two plus two has the same value as six.

John: I counted the middle set twice. I will move each top to the row only once.
Try together. Join one, one and one counter. Count all and say the number sentence.

2 + 1 = 3
Three books.

elements.text: Textbook (TB) and workbook (WB) page links refer to this chapter pair. All original tasks retain their prompt/answer meanings. Oral, pointing or practical demonstrations are valid; accept any clear dot arrangement.

TB2: JOIN-MODEL 2+1=3; the same three tops move. JOIN-GUIDED 1+1=2.
TB3: SIGNS-MODEL 2+1=3 and 3=2+1; both sides have value 3. SIGNS-GUIDED 1+2=3.
TB4: THREE-MODEL 1+1+2=4; 2+2+2=6. THREE-GUIDED 1+1+1=3.
TB5 / WB1: DRAW-MODEL 1+1=2; 2 books+1=3 books. DRAW-GUIDED draw 1 then 2 dots, total 3. WB-GUIDED first 2; then 3 dots, total 3.

TB6 / WB2-3 originals: Q1 1+2=3; Q2 2+2=4; Q3 1+1+1=3. Q4 two dots and one more, total 3. Q5 one dot and three more, total 4 books. Q6 draw 1+2 and 2+1; both total 3. Accept rearranged drawings with the correct counts and explanation.
TB7 / WB4-5: RECALL plus joins amounts; equals means same value; touch/count each once. HELP 1+1=2. RECHECK 2+1=3. SWAP both orders total 3 because no counter is added or removed.

TB8 / WB5-6: STORY 2+1=3 tops; all four take turns (not a top each). FRESH-TWO 1+3=4. FRESH-THREE 1+2+2=5. FRESH-EQUALS each side has value 4 or 5 respectively. Accept speech plus matching objects instead of fluent writing.
DELAYED, TB10: 2+2=4; 1+1+2=4; 4=2+2 is true.

textbook_pages.title: Teach, observe and revisit
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text: Suggested sessions: TB1-2 concrete joining; TB3 signs and equality; TB4 three sets; TB5 drawing; TB6 / WB2-3 independent tasks; TB7 help; TB8 and WB6 fresh checks. This is flexible editorial pacing, not an official timetable.

Read directions aloud. Use large safe counters or paper circles. Keep all materials reachable for seated participation. Allow touch, pointing, speech and drawing. Model the move into one row; do not introduce counting-on, carrying or totals through eighteen here.

Observe: Does the child preserve all objects, count each once, distinguish the separate sets from the total and read the entire number sentence? If a child counts a set twice, return to 1+1, moving each counter once into one row. Then use the new 2+1 recheck (TB7 / WB4). If equals is treated as an answer arrow, build 3 and 2+1 side by side and read 3=2+1.

Delayed recall, next session: Without showing earlier answers, ask the child to join two and two counters and record the total. Then join one, one and two. Ask whether 4=2+2 is true and why. Answers: 4; 4; yes, both sides have value 4. Record whether the child worked independently or with support.
Do not infer mastery from copied numerals. Return to concrete objects when needed.

elements.text: Glossary: set: a collection of objects. Join/add: put amounts together. Plus (+): the sign for adding. Total: how many altogether. Equals (=): has the same value as. Number sentence: numbers and signs that state a relationship.

Historical mapping: P1-p04-01: add two small sets, each 1 to 3, with total below 5. Core examples and Q1, Q2, Q4-Q6 keep that bound. Three-addend work is explicitly modelled (TB4); total 6 model and total 5 fresh check stay below 10. lessons.title: Count on to add
lessons.goal: Add two or three numbers with totals to 18.
lessons.look: The friends join sets. Can they start counting from the larger set?
lessons.learn: Keep one number in your head and count on the other amount. Adding zero leaves the number unchanged. Check by counting all the objects.
lessons.worked: 8 + 5: start at 8; count 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. So 8 + 5 = 13. For 3 + 2 + 4, first make 5, then add 4 to get 9.
lessons.play: Make sums with tops. First keep totals below 10, then try up to 18. A partner checks by grouping ten and ones.
lessons.hint: Keep every total within 18. Use objects before mental calculation.

elements.text: Page numbers here are PDF ordinals for adults; pupil links use printed titles. Any clear correct dot arrangement, oral explanation or practical demonstration is valid. Count-on words must begin AFTER the held number.

TB2 / WB1: COUNT-MODEL 4+2=6 (5,6); count all 6. COUNT-GUIDED 2+3=5 (3,4,5); all 5.
TB3 / WB1: THREE-SMALL-MODEL 3+2=5, then 5+4=9. THREE-SMALL-GUIDED 1+2+3=6; first 3, then 6. Each amount once.
TB4: ZERO-MODEL 6+0=6 and0+3=3; ZERO-GUIDED 5+0=5. Move nothing for zero.
TB5: CROSS-MODEL 8+5=13 (9..13); CROSS-GUIDED 7+4=11 (8..11). Count-all checks 13 and 11.

TB6 / TB9 / WB5: THREE-LARGE-MODEL 4+5+6=15: hold 4, count 5..9, then 10..15. THREE-LARGE-GUIDED 9+0+8=17: still 9, then 10..17. S005 exact answers 15 and 17, all three addends once; correct count-on or count-all demonstration.
TB7 / WB4: CHECK-MODEL 8+6=14, six new count words 9..14; incorrect 13 repeats starting 8. Count all 14. CHECK-GUIDED 5+2=7 (6,7); wrong 6 is one too few.
TB8 / WB2-4 originals: Q1=7; Q2=6; Q3=8 (first 5, then 8); Q4=18; Q5=12 seeds; Q6 count all 14 objects OR count on six from 8 (9..14). Both are valid; comparing both methods strengthens checking.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter nine / Count on to add
textbook_pages.title: Support, fresh checks and recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text:
TB10 / WB6-7: RECALL first new word is the next number after held start; zero adds none; count-all checks. HELP 2+1=3 (say 3); RECHECK 3+2=5 (4,5), then count all 5.
TB11 / WB7: STORY 8+5=13, count 9..13; all 13 original counters conserved. The printed pictures are a model of the same inventory, not extra counters.

TB12 / WB8: FRESH-TWO 5+7=12 (6..12); FRESH-THREE 2+0+9=11 (still 2, then 3..11); FRESH-CHECK 6+3=9, claim 8 is false;7,8,9 and all 9. Equals means same value on both sides. Accept counters, dots and oral explanations, with accurate totals.

Suggested teaching: distribute TB2-7 over short sessions with movement and turns. If the held number is counted again, use TB10 two-plus-one intervention and different three-plus-two recheck. If a third set is missed, keep it separate until its turn. For zero, point to an empty space and move no object. Do not introduce column addition or counting beyond 18 here.

DELAYED next session: Cover earlier answers. Privately give six counters and five more: 11. Then three, zero and seven: 10. Ask whether 7+2=8 is true: no, correct 9. Ask the child to count on and then check all. Record independence/support. Read aloud and accept pointing, speech or seated action.

elements.text: Glossary: count on: keep a known amount and say the next numbers for added objects. Sum/total: how many altogether. Addend (adult term): an amount being added. Zero: no objects in the set. Check: use a method to see whether a result is right. Equals (=): has the same value as.

Historical mapping: P1-p04-02 two/three addends below 10; P1-p04-03 two/three totals through 18 under the documented inclusive provisional bound; P1-p04-05 checking accuracy. S005 retained exactly. elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Keep the story pencils aside. Use paper strips for practice. Each strip stands for one pencil. Count the ten strips in a tied bundle. The two ties do not stand for pencils.
Tens
Ones

One bundle and two loose strips make twelve.
12 = 1 ten and 2 ones.
The left digit tells the tens. The right digit tells the ones. Put bundles in the tens place and loose strips in the ones place.
Try together: build 14 with paper strips. Point to its tens and ones. Say what each digit means.

Ones
Tens
Ones

Add the ones: 2 + 5 = 7.
Add the tens: 1 ten + 1 ten = 2 tens.
12 + 15 = 27.
The seven ones stay loose. We have fewer than ten ones, so we do not make another bundle. Untie the two bundles and count all 27 strips to check.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Write each digit in its place. Tens go under tens. Ones go under ones. Add the ones first. Then add the tens.
Tens
Ones

The line separates the amounts from their total. The plus sign means add. The equals sign means the same value.
12 + 15 = 27
Try together: build 11 and 12. Adamu moves the ones. Grace moves the tens. Say the total. In your workbook or exercise book, write the sum with like places lined up.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Thirty has three tens and zero ones. Ten has one ten and zero ones. Zero tells us that the ones place is empty.

Ones

0 + 0 = 0 ones. 3 tens + 1 ten = 4 tens.
30 + 10 = 40. No loose ones.
Build it with four bundles. Untie and count all 40 strips to check. Keep the zero when you write 40: four means four ones; forty means four tens.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Add 14 and 5. Five is five ones and no tens. Put the 5 under the 4, in the ones place. Leave the tens place in that row empty.

Ones

4 + 5 = 9 ones. 1 ten + no tens = 1 ten.
14 + 5 = 19.

Aishatu: I nearly put the 5 in the tens place. I will wait and check its place first.
John: Five loose strips belong with the loose strips. Build 14 and 5, join, then count all 19 to check.

textbook_pages.title: Answers to every task
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text: Adult record: PDF page ordinals below; stable IDs are not pupil numbering. Accept correct drawings in any arrangement, spoken explanations or practical demonstrations. A bundle must contain ten ones. Count each strip once in an all-ones check.

TB2 PLACE: 12 is 1 ten and 2 ones; guided 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones.
TB3 JOIN-MODEL / TB4 COLUMN-MODEL: 12+15=27; 2+5=7 ones, 1+1=2 tens; untie/count all 27.
TB4 / WB1 GUIDED: 11+12=23; 1+2=3 ones, 1+1=2 tens; check all 23.
TB5 LARGE-MODEL: 23+14=37; 3+4=7 ones, 2+1=3 tens; check all 37.

TB6 ZERO-MODEL: 30+10=40; zero ones and four tens; count 40 unbundled strips. ZERO-GUIDED: 20+13=33; 3 ones, 3 tens.
TB7 ONE-DIGIT-MODEL / WB3 Q4: 14+5=19; 5 under 4 in ones; 9 ones, 1 ten; count 19.
TB8 CHECK-MODEL: 12+11=23, not 24. TB8 / WB5 CHECK-GUIDED: 13+12=25, not 24. Rebuild/join/count all to check.

TB9 / WB2-4 source questions: Q1 25; Q2 37; Q3 40; Q4 19; Q5 33 pencils; Q6 two tens plus one ten and three ones make three tens and three ones. These retain all six original prompts and answer meanings.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter ten / Add tens and ones
textbook_pages.title: Support, checks and delayed recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text:
TB10 / WB6: RECALL tens under tens, ones under ones; add ones then tens; check by joining and counting all unbundled strips. HELP 10+2=12; RECHECK 10+4=14. Use a different fresh recheck after any extra demonstration.
TB11 STORY / WB4 Q5: 22+11=33 pencils; three tens and three ones. Original stock is conserved; practice strips are separate.

TB12 / WB7 fresh: FRESH-TWO 24+13=37 (7 ones,3 tens). FRESH-ZERO 20+20=40 (0 ones,4 tens). FRESH-CHECK 12+5=17, not 62; align the 5 under the 2 as ones, not under the 1 as tens. EXPLAIN: ones totals 7,0,7 are below ten, so no new bundle. Independent all-ones checks give 37,40,17.

Suggested sessions and misconceptions: teach TB2-4, then TB5-7, then TB8-12 in several short sessions. Give all four children turns. If 5 is placed in tens, physically put five loose strips in ones. If 40 becomes 4, contrast four loose strips with four actual bundles. If needed return to TB10, then its fresh 10+4 recheck.

DELAYED next session: Cover all earlier printed and handwritten answers. Give 13+16 (29), 20+10 (30), then the claim 21+7=91 (false:28). Ask for aligned recording and a build/join/count-all check. Record independence and support.

textbook_pages.title: Words, evidence and next learning
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text: Glossary: ten: a group of ten ones. One: a single item. Place: a digit's position in a number. Total/sum: how many altogether. Add (+): join amounts. Equals (=): has the same value as. Check: use a method to see whether an answer is right.

Historical curriculum mapping: P1-p04-04: add two-digit numbers without regrouping, total at most 40. This chapter also rehearses P1-p04-05 checking accuracy, including the totals 23 and 25 deferred from Chapter 9. Core objective, original Q1-Q6 and complete old-to-new answer map are in canonical production/p1.json. Single-digit addends are deliberate place-value bridging practice.

lessons.title: Take away
lessons.look: Musa puts some tops back in a box. Is the number on his mat getting larger or smaller?
lessons.learn: Subtraction can take away. The sign − means subtract. Count what remains. Or count backwards one step per removed object.
lessons.play: Place up to 18 tops on a mat. A partner removes some while you watch. Say the subtraction and check by putting them back.
lessons.hint: Keep removed objects visible so pupils can undo the action.

questions.prompt: 12 chalk pieces: use 3. How many remain?

lessons.title: Find a missing part
lessons.goal: Find unknown numbers and check everyday calculations.
lessons.look: Amina sees 3 tops. Some are hidden. There are 7 altogether. How can she find the hidden part?
lessons.learn: A blank stands for a missing number. Find the value that makes both sides equal. Use objects or count on. Check by reading the completed sentence.
lessons.worked: 3 + __ = 7: count 4 more. The blank is 4. __ − 2 = 5: start with 7, since 7 − 2 = 5.
lessons.play: Hide part of a set of up to 9 tops. Tell the whole and the visible part. Then make an everyday story about books with a missing amount.
lessons.hint: Vary blank positions. Check by substituting in the original sentence.

questions.answer: Use 5 in the blank and verify 4 + 5 = 9.

lessons.title: Pretend coins and change
lessons.goal: Identify coin values and calculate with pretend kobo.
lessons.look: Daniel makes paper tokens for a pretend shop. Why does a value label matter?
lessons.learn: Nigerian money is called naira and kobo. 100 kobo = 1 naira. Use labelled pretend tokens: 1k, 5k, 10k and 25k. These are historical-value exercises, not real prices or a claim about money circulating today.
lessons.worked: 5k + 10k = 15k. Pay 10k for a pretend 6k item: change is 10k − 6k = 4k.
lessons.play: Draw token outlines and label values. An adult may show a genuine coin for identification and supervised pencil tracing. Never mark or alter real money.
lessons.hint: Use large paper tokens. Real prices and currently used denominations differ.

questions.prompt: Why read a token value, not just count tokens?
questions.answer: Different tokens can have different values.

lessons.title: Longer, shorter and farther
lessons.goal: Compare and order lengths and measure with body units.
lessons.look: Zainab compares two strings for a garden bed. Where should their ends start?
lessons.learn: Line up one end to compare. Longer means more length; shorter means less. Measure with equal hand spans or footsteps placed end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
lessons.worked: One string is 4 of Amina’s spans; another is 6 of her spans. The second is longer by 2 of her spans.
lessons.play: Measure a table in your spans and a safe path in your steps. Record whose units you used. A seated child can use a paper strip instead.
lessons.hint: Body units vary. Do not compare different pupils’ counts as if their spans were equal.

questions.prompt: Lengths are 3 and 5 equal strips. Which is longer?
Draw a line longer than your finger.
questions.answer: Line exceeds that pupil’s finger length.

questions.prompt: A path is 8 steps out and 8 back. Total?
Measure a book with repeated paper-strip units.
questions.answer: Practical count, same unit repeated without gaps.

questions.prompt: Why line up the string ends?
questions.answer: So the other ends show the difference fairly.

lessons.title: Our day in order
lessons.goal: Sequence everyday activities and use time words.
lessons.look: The friends describe a school day. What could you do before coming to school?
lessons.learn: Time helps order events. Morning comes before afternoon. Evening comes before night. Routines differ. Use before and after to describe a day.
lessons.worked: In Amina’s story: wake up, wash, eat, then go to school. Eating is before going to school.
lessons.play: Draw three routine cards. A partner puts them in your chosen order. Tell a story using first, next and last.
lessons.hint: Accept varied home routines. No pupil must disclose private home details.

questions.prompt: Which comes first: morning or afternoon?
In Amina’s story, what follows washing?
Explain before with your own two events.
questions.answer: The first event occurs earlier than the second.

lessons.title: Heavy and light
lessons.look: Musa lifts an empty bag and a bag with books. Which feels heavier?
lessons.learn: Heavier and lighter compare weight. Size alone does not tell weight. Use small safe objects on a simple balance. The lower pan holds the heavier load.
lessons.worked: On a balance, a stone side goes down and a leaf side goes up. The stone is heavier than the leaf.
lessons.play: With an adult, balance a small stone, eraser and leaf. Predict, compare and order. Lift only light safe items.
lessons.hint: Never ask pupils to lift heavy loads. Use observed results, not appearance.

questions.prompt: Which is heavier in the example?
Which is lighter in the example?

questions.answer: Suitable example such as a leaf.

questions.prompt: A balance is level. What can this show?
Compare two safe objects and record a result.
Does bigger always mean heavier? Explain.
questions.answer: No; a large empty box can be lighter than a small stone.

lessons.title: Solid shapes around us
lessons.goal: Name and sort cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres.
lessons.look: Daniel explores a ball, a box and a closed tin. Which can roll?
lessons.learn: A sphere is ball-shaped. A cube has six equal square faces. A cuboid has six rectangular faces, with opposite faces matching. A cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface.
lessons.worked: A dice models a cube; a cereal box models a cuboid; a closed straight-sided tin models a cylinder; a ball models a sphere.
lessons.play: Sort clean safe objects by solid shape. Test rolling and stacking. Remove sharp tins and small choking hazards.
lessons.hint: A cube is a special cuboid. Use a clear non-cube cuboid for initial comparison.

questions.prompt: What solid does a ball model?
Which solid has six equal square faces?
What solid does a closed straight-sided tin model?
Sort a ball and box by smooth rolling.
questions.answer: Ball rolls smoothly; box does not.
Cube edges are all equal; the chosen non-cube cuboid has unequal adjacent edge lengths.

lessons.title: Flat shapes and patterns
lessons.goal: Match and name circles, squares and rectangles.
lessons.look: Amina traces a box face. How does the flat drawing differ from the box?
lessons.learn: A circle has a curved boundary and no corners. A square has 4 equal straight sides and 4 square corners. A rectangle has 4 square corners and opposite sides equal. A square is a special rectangle.
lessons.worked: Circle, square, circle, square is a repeating pattern. A turned square is still a square.
lessons.play: Trace safe flat faces. Match shapes after turning them. Make a repeating pattern for a pretend cloth border. Find square and rectangular faces in the classroom.
lessons.hint: Orientation does not change a shape. Compare with a non-square rectangle.

questions.prompt: How many corners has a circle?
How many equal sides has a square?

questions.answer: Four right angles, opposite equal sides, unequal adjacent lengths.

questions.prompt: Name an object with a rectangular face.
questions.answer: Suitable example such as a book.

questions.prompt: What stays the same when a square turns?
questions.answer: Its four equal sides and four right-angle corners.

lessons.title: Find out about our class
lessons.goal: Collect and record ages and heights.
lessons.look: The friends discuss how children grow. What could they record respectfully?
lessons.learn: Data are pieces of information. Ask the same question each time. Record age in completed years. Compare heights from floor to head with marked paper strips. Use letters instead of names.
lessons.worked: Invented practice data: pupil A is 6 years, B is 7, C is 6. Two pupils are 6 years old.
lessons.play: Use the invented records or collect voluntary ages privately. Compare paper height strips without ranking children as better or worse. Record height with a consistent method.
lessons.hint: Participation is optional. Do not publish identifiable child data. Fictional data are acceptable.

questions.prompt: How old is practice pupil B?
Order the practice ages from least.
Name a tool for comparing heights.
questions.answer: Marked paper strip or suitable measuring tape

questions.prompt: Why ask everyone the same age question?
questions.answer: To compare answers about the same thing.

stages.S1: Textbook 5: Mrs Binta introduces Aishatu's pretend tea-shop cup problem from the classroom blackboard, four seated children facing her; each of the four friends needs a cup. The board hint Touch one. Say one number. motivates the counting method without numerals.
stages.S2: Textbook 5: We will count, read, write and order one to five. Numerals are not required before concrete modelling.
stages.S3: Textbook 6: Mrs Binta touches three cups once each, says one/two/three and states the total; textbook 7 links exact sets 1-5 to numerals and models two cups/two circles. Textbook 9 and adult 18 require live numeral formation before workbook tracing.
stages.S4: Textbook 6-7: Aishatu slows down, Grace checks, pupils touch/count with the teacher, and John asks whether a drawing can represent a cup. Adult 18 requires real-cup enactment and guided turns.
stages.S5: Textbook 8-9 / workbook 2-4: all six source tasks independently count 3/5 cups, draw 2 circles, write 1-5, show 4 and demonstrate counting once. Workbook has local diagrams and ample response spaces; exercise-book alternatives are explicit.
stages.S6: Textbook 9 / workbook 4: recall Mrs Binta before looking back; show four, then explain/show how to avoid Adamu's repeat count on a three-cup set.
stages.S7: Textbook 9 and adult 18: smaller step uses two real cups moved aside once per number word, then a fresh small set; adult guidance also separates total, numeral recognition/reading and formation difficulties.
stages.S8: Textbook 10 / adult 19: four portraits and four exact cup drawings give each friend a cup; enact this pairing with real cups before the closing dialogue opens the shop.
stages.S9: Textbook 10 / workbook 5 / adult 18-19: adult-selected 1-5 physical set and drawing; shuffled numeral recognition followed by separate mixed-order numeral naming without giving the value. Another-day fresh two-or-five-object total and shuffled recognition supplied.
